title: I asked Gemini and Claude to build a no-code subscription tracker
excerpt: I gave Gemini and Claude the same prompt to build a no-code subscription tracker. Both worked at first, but only one survived a small change.
content_html:
Published Nov 21, 2026, 8:45 AM EST

Haroun authors features for Android Police, covering Android, Samsung, Google, and AI. He first joined in 2021, writing over 200 news stories before moving on to features and how-tos. A one-time OnePlus die-hard who genuinely couldn't stand Samsung, he's since done a full about-face — he now daily-drives a Galaxy S24 Ultra and keeps an S23+, S22+, and his old S20 within arm's reach, which gives him a lot of hardware to put through its paces.

He also holds a medical degree (MBBS) and has been obsessed with consumer tech for more than a decade. His work has appeared on How-To Geek and Android Authority. When he's not buried in Google's apps or a Samsung settings menu, he's trying to get his chess rating past 1500 or reading up on genetics and preventive medicine.

I've had to enter my card details to register for free trials.

I've even paid a month's subscription for a tool I didn't intend to use after that. And I often forgot to cancel.

As a result, I've had my fair share of unexpected charges, and I've tried different solutions, like using an empty card for free trials.

But I use tools fairly often that require a funded card. And I'd ideally love to see all of them, with their billing dates, in one place.

However, I don't want to download or pay for an app to monitor the other apps I pay for, so I decided to create one myself with AI.

I asked Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude to build a subscription tracker that shows my monthly and yearly spend, flags anything renewing in the next seven days, and saves my changes.

Only one of them created something I'd actually use. Let me explain.

Both chatbots aced the build on the first try

I switched to Gemini's most powerful Argon model and gave it a single prompt with all the features I wanted.

It built everything in Canvas, which is probably the best Google tool you're not using.

It also added nifty features like a search bar, a sort menu, filters for monthly and yearly plans, a Roll to Next Cycle button for each subscription, and a bar that splits my spending between monthly and yearly plans.

It even gave the build a name, SubPulse, which I found really cool.

Claude kept it simple

Claude's build was simpler than Gemini's.

It stuck to what I asked for and added only what was needed to make the build functional.

For example, it added automatic rollover even though I didn't ask for it. So, when a renewal date passes, the tracker automatically moves that item to the next month or year.

Both worked as intended

While prompting the chatbots, I included some sample subscription data.

Everything displayed correctly, and the math added up.

I then played around with the buttons, like adding, deleting, or editing items on the tracker, and everything worked fine.

At this point, the only differences were Gemini's extra features and the design. And I liked Gemini's version.

A small change broke one of the builds

Gemini went blank

The builds were already good, but I wanted to make them even better.

I asked both AI tools to add a dark mode toggle and a notes field to each subscription. But when I opened Gemini's build, it showed a blank page.

The code was still there, but I assumed it was broken, so I asked Gemini to fix it. It found and removed some stray code, but it still didn't work.

After repeated prompting and trying completely new builds in new chats that also broke, I gave up.

Claude breezed through the edits

I gave Claude the same request to add a dark mode toggle and a notes field to each subscription.

The final build opened just fine, worked correctly, and saved all my changes.

At this point, Claude was ahead, because I couldn't see Gemini's build on my phone. But Gemini got close again toward the end.

One tracker looks better on my home screen

Claude's tracker works perfectly

There's no point in a build if I have to dig through a sea of chats to use it.

The builds need to be easily accessible. So I generated a link for my Claude build, opened it in Chrome, and created a shortcut on my home screen.

Tapping the shortcut takes me to the tracker in Chrome.

I particularly like that the shortcut has a unique icon, so it feels like a different tool rather than a Claude extension.

And any change I make on the web version syncs with the build inside Claude.

Gemini's tracker works, with some annoyances

I initially thought the Gemini build was broken after it failed to preview.

However, when I generated a link to the build and opened it in Chrome, it previewed fine. But repeated attempts to fix it had removed my edits.

As with Claude, I created a home screen shortcut that took me straight to the build.

The first thing I noticed was the rather boring letter "G" icon that did a poor job of making my build stand out.

Also, the web preview didn't display full screen. For some reason, the top quarter of the display was empty, which worsened the experience.

I also noticed that my changes in the web version didn't carry over to the build in the Gemini app.

I'm keeping Claude's tracker

I liked Gemini's build. It had more features, and the design appealed to me more. But after it started breaking, I gravitated toward Claude.

Getting them onto my home screen settled it. Claude's tracker has the better icon and a full-screen view.

If you'd rather cut down on your subscriptions, replace paid apps with open source alternatives.
